title: China Holds Unannounced Pacific Drills That Taiwan Calls Silent Intimidation
excerpt: Taiwanese officials told Reuters more than 100 Chinese vessels took part in early-November drills around Taiwan and across the western Pacific. Beijing has called its carrier activity routine and did not respond to Reuters on the wider deployment.
body:
• China carried out a large, unannounced military exercise across the western Pacific and around Taiwan in early November, Taiwanese officials told Reuters.
  • A senior Taiwan security official said more than 100 Chinese military and coast guard vessels were massed at one point, in drills that included simulated attacks — a deployment the official said was larger than Justice Mission 2025.
  • Taiwan's defence minister Wellington Koo described the activity as "area denial" drills; China has said its carrier is on routine exercises not directed at any country, and its defence ministry did not respond to Reuters.
  • The vessel count inside the first island chain had fallen to about 70 by Friday, according to two Taiwan security officials.

China carried out a large, unannounced military exercise across the western Pacific and around Taiwan in early November, in what officials in Taipei described to Reuters as a campaign of "silent intimidation" aimed at pressuring Taiwan and other governments before major international meetings. The description is Taipei's characterisation, attributed to the officials who spoke to Reuters, not a label China accepts.

A senior Taiwan security official, speaking on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the matter, said China's military and coast guard had at one point massed more than 100 vessels in the region early this month, conducting drills that included simulated attacks on other militaries and cities, including Taiwan's. The official said the deployment was larger than Justice Mission 2025, China's last formally named drills targeting Taiwan nearly a year ago, and one of the largest Chinese naval deployments to date.

"It is a silent exercise — and in effect, silent intimidation."

— Senior Taiwan security official, speaking to Reuters on condition of anonymity

What the drills involved, according to Taipei

The official said the drills involved coordinated naval forces from China's eastern, northern and southern theatre commands — a scale that, in the official's assessment, suggested Beijing was rehearsing not only a Taiwan blockade scenario but broader operations across the western Pacific, and working to integrate regional fleets into a single far-seas force. During the drills, a Chinese submarine also launched an intercontinental ballistic missile from the Yellow Sea into the Chinese mainland, the official said. Reuters did not report independent confirmation of the simulated-attack details, and they are presented here as the Taiwan official's account.

A foreign intelligence source told Reuters the unnamed drills appeared deliberate, allowing Beijing to apply pressure while avoiding a diplomatic backlash.

By this week the scale had decreased. About 70 vessels were operating within the first island chain on Friday, according to two Taiwan security officials. Taiwan National Security Council Secretary-General Joseph Wu posted on X late on Thursday that, while the number of vessels had decreased, the groups of the Northern, Eastern and Southern Theatre Commands plus the Liaoning carrier strike group remained operating in waters east of the Philippines, and that Chinese air force activity near Taiwan remained high.

How Beijing and Taipei's ministry describe it

China's defence ministry did not respond to a Reuters request for comment on the first report. Taiwan's defence ministry referred Reuters to comments by Defence Minister Wellington Koo this week, saying China was carrying out "area denial" drills in the western Pacific involving an aircraft carrier and other naval formations — drills Koo described in a separate Reuters analysis as aimed at stopping US or other allied forces from coming to Taipei's aid if Beijing attacked. China, which has never renounced the use of force to bring Taiwan under its control, has said the carrier is on routine exercises that are not directed at any country.

China views democratically governed Taiwan as its own territory and has stepped up military pressure over the past five years, drawing condemnation from Taipei. On Thursday, Chinese President Xi Jinping gave a major policy speech about Taiwan urging peaceful "reunification," though making no mention of using force, Reuters reported. China's state-backed Global Times said on Friday that if Taiwan's ruling party persists in seeking independence by relying on external forces or military means, it would face a harsh reckoning.

Timing before APEC

The timing sits ahead of a major diplomatic week. Beijing is hosting the APEC leaders' summit in Shenzhen next week, where US President Donald Trump and Xi are expected to meet for the third time this year, and Taiwan also attends APEC. In Taipei's reading, set out by its officials to Reuters, conducting a large exercise without a name or announcement lets Beijing signal strength to Taiwan and to governments that might support it, while limiting the diplomatic cost that a formally announced exercise would carry. Whether that was Beijing's intent has not been confirmed by China, whose public position remains that the activity is routine training.
